nodes.label: Nechaev: deterministic generic DLP needs Omega(sqrt r)
nodes.statement: In Nechaev's model (equality of represented elements testable without an oracle query), every deterministic generic algorithm for DLP in a group of prime order r needs Omega(sqrt r) time and space.
nodes.scope: Deterministic algorithms only, so it does not cover Pollard rho or any randomized method; Shoup 1997 removed that restriction.
non_implications: Gives no bound on randomized algorithms such as rho or kangaroo

nodes.label: Maurer register-based generic model
nodes.statement: Group elements live in registers of a black box with no external labels; the algorithm issues operation queries O(op, i1..i_t+1) and relation queries (e.g. equality) and must output a function of the register contents.
nodes.scope: Rho and BSGS are not expressible without an extra well-ordering relation oracle; the Shoup-style lower bound transfers only if equality-query cost is ignored or a total order is allowed (Galbraith 13.4.2-13.4.3).

nodes.label: Shoup vs Maurer generic models differ on multi-stage games
nodes.statement: Constructions captured by Maurer's model are captured by Shoup's; for single-stage games the two security notions coincide, but for some multi-stage games Shoup-model security is strictly stronger; there are new un-instantiability results for Maurer's model.
nodes.scope: Model-theoretic; it says which generic lower bounds may be quoted in which model, not anything about concrete curves.
non_implications: Does not change the single-target DLP birthday bound, a single-stage game

nodes.label: Generic group plus random oracle model (Schnorr-Jakobsson)
nodes.statement: A combined idealization in which the adversary is generic for the group and the hash function is a random oracle; Schnorr and Jakobsson prove signed ElGamal secure against adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack in it.
nodes.scope: Proofs in this joint model inherit both idealizations; they say nothing about adversaries that use curve coordinates or hash structure.

nodes.label: Algebraic group model (FKL 2018)
nodes.statement: An algebraic algorithm must output, with every group element it produces, a representation of it as a linear combination of the group elements it received; it may otherwise use the group representation.
nodes.scope: Sits between the standard model and the GGM; hardness statements are relative to DL, not unconditional.

nodes.label: FKL: CDH, SDH, LRSW equivalent to DL in the AGM
nodes.statement: In the algebraic group model, computational Diffie-Hellman, strong Diffie-Hellman and interactive LRSW are each equivalent to the discrete logarithm problem; BLS signatures and Groth16 get tight reductions to (a variant of) DL.
nodes.scope: Equivalences hold only against algebraic adversaries; ECDLP hardness itself remains assumed.

nodes.label: FKL transfer: AGM results plus GGM DL bound give GGM bounds
nodes.statement: Combining AGM reductions to DL with the generic DL lower bound yields generic-group lower bounds for the reduced assumptions (CDH, SDH, LRSW, ...).
nodes.scope: Disputed: Katz-Zhang-Zhou 2022 show it fails under the current formalizations; Jaeger-Mohan give an interpretation under which it holds for most algebraic analyses. Treat any GGM bound obtained this way as conditional on that interpretation.
assumptions: The Jaeger-Mohan interpretation of algebraic and generic models

nodes.label: KZZ: AGM is not (as formalized) weaker than the GGM
nodes.statement: Under the current formalizations, hardness against algebraic algorithms need not imply hardness against generic algorithms, and a generic reduction in the AGM need not yield one in the GGM.
nodes.scope: A statement about model formalizations, with explicit separating cases in the paper (not read).

nodes.label: Jaeger-Mohan: AGM proofs transfer to the GGM under general frameworks
nodes.statement: Within general frameworks for generic and algebraic models over arbitrary algebraic structures, the FKL-style transfer from AGM hardness to GGM hardness is correct, and most algebraic analyses in the literature fall within those frameworks.
nodes.scope: Restores the transfer under a specific interpretation; analyses outside the frameworks remain uncovered.

nodes.label: Zhandry: un-instantiability in the AGM
nodes.statement: There are schemes secure in the algebraic group model that cannot be securely instantiated with any concrete group (a new un-instantiability result for the AGM).
nodes.scope: Like random-oracle un-instantiability results, it targets contrived constructions; it is a limit on reading AGM proofs as concrete security, not an attack on ECDLP.

nodes.label: Yun: generic n-target DLP needs Omega(sqrt(n p))
nodes.statement: Solving n discrete logarithms simultaneously in a group of prime order p requires, for generic algorithms, a number of group operations matching the known O(sqrt(n p)) algorithms up to constants, proved via a search-by-hyperplane-queries problem.
nodes.scope: Generic model, no preprocessing; the admissible range of n (relaxed in a revision) was not read.

nodes.label: Kuhn-Struik: L targets with one DP table in about sqrt(2 r L)
nodes.statement: Keeping the distinguished points of earlier solves (rewriting g^a h_i^b as g^a' once log h_i is known) solves L DLP instances (1 < L < r^(1/4)) in roughly sqrt(2 r L) group operations; the expected number of samples to see k collisions is about sqrt(2 k N) (their Theorem 1).
nodes.scope: Random-mapping analysis. Hitchcock-Montague-Carter-Dawson: the walk function must not depend on the targets h_i (only the start points may).
failure_modes: A walk that depends on h_i loses the shared-table collisions

nodes.label: CDG: auxiliary-input GGM bounds via presampling
nodes.statement: In the auxiliary-input generic-group model (the attacker may leak a bounded-length function of the encoding table), simpler proofs recover the Corrigan-Gibbs-Kogan preprocessing bounds for DL and DH-type problems and add bounds for two further assumptions.
nodes.scope: Same idealization as CGK; formulas and constants not read here.

nodes.label: AHP: GGM bounds via geometric-search reductions (with preprocessing)
nodes.statement: Reducing a broad class of problems to geometric search problems, then to search-by-hypersurface with known information-theoretic bounds, gives generic lower bounds with and without preprocessing (bit-fixing AI-GGM), reproving several results previously obtained via the AGM.
nodes.scope: Generic and bit-fixing preprocessing models only.

nodes.label: Bernstein-Lange precomputed-DP rho: ~ell^(1/3) online
nodes.statement: With t = ceil(log2(ell)/3), precompute about ell^(1/3) distinguished points each ending a walk of length at least 2^t (covering about ell^(2/3) points, precomputation on the scale of ell^(2/3): 2^170 for P-256). An online walk from aP + bQ succeeds within 2^(t+1) steps with probability at least about (1 - 1/e)/e = 0.23, so the online cost is about 2 ell^(1/3) additions and success p costs about (p ell)^(1/3) in the RAM and NAND metrics; in the AT metric the cost is about (p ell)^(1/2), no better than rho.
nodes.scope: Non-uniform: the table is free advice. Random-walk heuristics plus their own experiments (in the small-DL paper) for the O constants. Does not exploit any curve property.
assumptions: Random-walk heuristic for the precomputed walks
Free precomputation of about ell^(2/3) steps
nodes.formula: online ~ 2 ell^(1/3); RAM cost (p ell)^(1/3); AT cost (p ell)^(1/2)
non_implications: No gain in the AT (area-time) metric
Precomputation is far above sqrt(ell), so no improvement for a single uniform attacker

cited_by.note: implements the N^(2/3)-precomputation / N^(1/3)-online cost model

nodes.label: BL small DL: 1.77 ell^(1/3) with a table of ell^(1/3)
nodes.statement: Experimentally, a table of size ell^(1/3) precomputed with 1.24 ell^(2/3) multiplications solves a DLP in a group of order ell with 1.77 ell^(1/3) multiplications on average (interval of order ell: 1.93 ell^(1/3) with 1.21 ell^(2/3) precomputation); it improves the Lee-Cheon-Hong parameter choice (their a = 0.809 gives 2.058 (ell/T)^(1/2); a = 1.5 gives 2 (ell/T)^(1/2) under the same heuristics).
nodes.scope: Constants are measurements on chosen sizes; the authors recommend tuning alpha experimentally rather than trusting the heuristic analysis. Generic only through free precomputation.
nodes.formula: 1.77 ell^(1/3) online, table ell^(1/3), precomputation 1.24 ell^(2/3)

nodes.label: Rigorous rho analyses assume a uniformly random partition
nodes.statement: Each group element is assigned independently and uniformly to a walk branch (the selection function S is a random function / random oracle); under this assumption the deterministic iteration is a Markov chain until its first repeat.
nodes.scope: Not implementable in polynomial storage: a key of c log2 r bits yields at most r^c partitions, against at least 6^(r/3) equal three-way partitions, so the rigorous theorems do not apply to the algorithm as implemented (Galbraith 14.2.5).

nodes.label: DP rho heuristic (Galbraith Heur. 14.2.15 / Thm 14.2.16)
nodes.statement: Assume walks reach a distinguished point in far fewer than sqrt r steps (no cycles) and that the expected number of sampled elements before a collision is sqrt(pi r/2); then rho with distinguished points needs (sqrt(pi/2) + o(1)) sqrt r = (1.253 + o(1)) sqrt r group operations, versus (3.093 + o(1)) sqrt r with Floyd cycle finding (Heuristic 14.2.10, epact 0.823 sqrt(pi r/2)).
nodes.scope: Galbraith notes the heuristic is essentially equivalent to the conclusion it is used to prove; its support is experimental.
nodes.formula: E[T] = (1.253 + o(1)) sqrt r (DP); (3.093 + o(1)) sqrt r (Floyd)

nodes.label: Miller-Venkatesan: rho graph mixes in O(log^3 n) thanks to squaring
nodes.statement: For the original three-branch walk x -> gx, hx, x^2 on a cyclic group of prime order n with a random partition, the operator-norm spectral analysis gives mixing time O((log n)^3); without the squaring step the mixing time would be exponential in log n. The result extends to any fixed number of multiplier branches plus x -> x^r with gcd(r, n) = 1.
nodes.scope: Random-partition model. The squaring (EC doubling) branch is essential to the proof; pure additive (r-adding) walks used in practice are not covered.
source_locations: Miller-Venkatesan 2006 abstract, Proposition 3.2 and following Remark
Miller-Venkatesan 2006, 'Generalizations' after the proof of Theorem 1.1
non_implications: Says nothing about r-adding walks without a squaring/doubling branch
Collision does not imply a nondegenerate relation (separate paper)

nodes.label: Miller-Venkatesan: rho collisions are nondegenerate
nodes.statement: For the three-branch rho walk on a group of prime order n with random start g^r1 h^r2, if the multiplicative order of 2 mod n is at least c0 (log n)^3, any collision before time T is nondegenerate with probability at least 1 - O(T^2/n^2); in particular the O(sqrt n) collisions are nondegenerate with probability 1 - O(1/n). At most O((log X)^5) primes in [X, 2X] violate the order condition, and replacing squaring by x -> x^l for a suitable prime l = O((log n)^6 log log n) makes the analysis unconditional.
nodes.scope: Random-partition model and random start; degeneracies in the first steps from a fixed start are not ruled out.

nodes.label: Kim-Montenegro-Tetali: rho collision in O(sqrt|G| log|G| loglog|G|)
nodes.statement: For the three-branch rho walk with a random partition, a collision occurs with high probability within O(sqrt(|G|) log|G| log log|G|) steps; the walk on the exponent cycle Z_N (u -> u+1, u+x, 2u, each with probability 1/3) mixes in O(log|G| log log|G|).
nodes.scope: Superseded by KMPT 2010 (Theta(sqrt|G|)); canonical-path, log-Sobolev and spectral-profile methods cannot go below O(log^2 |G|) mixing for this walk.

nodes.label: KMPT: birthday paradox for Markov chains
nodes.statement: For a finite ergodic Markov chain with uniform stationary distribution on N states, O(sqrt N) steps suffice for a self-intersection provided the relative pointwise (L-infinity) distance to stationarity drops steadily early in the walk; the bound is additive (C sqrt N plus a mixing term) rather than sqrt N times a mixing time.
nodes.scope: General probability theorem; its rho application needs the random-partition model.

nodes.label: KMPT: rho collides in Theta(sqrt|G|), constant <= 52.5
nodes.statement: For every starting state, the expected number of steps of the three-branch rho walk (random-oracle partition) before a collision is at most (1 + o(1)) 12 sqrt(19) sqrt|G| < (1 + o(1)) 52.5 sqrt|G|; for van Oorschot-Wiener distinguished points on J processors, Theta(sqrt(|G|)/J) steps suffice.
nodes.scope: Order-optimal (matches Shoup) but the proved constant is about 42 times the heuristic sqrt(pi/2) = 1.2533; random partition only; collision, not nondegenerate collision (nondegeneracy from Miller-Venkatesan 2008).
non_implications: Does not prove the sqrt(pi/2) constant
Does not cover r-adding walks or a fixed cheap hash partition

nodes.label: Brent-Pollard nonrandomness: factor 1/sqrt(1 - sum p_i^2)
nodes.statement: A walk that is injective on each branch with branch probabilities p_i needs about 1/sqrt(1 - sum_i p_i^2) times the random-mapping collision time; for r-adding walks with p_i = 1/r this is 1/sqrt(1 - 1/r) (equivalently expected cycle length c sqrt(pi r/2) with c^2 = r/(r-1), Brent-Pollard, Arney-Bender, Blackburn-Murphy, Teske).
nodes.scope: Accounts only for degree-1 local anti-collisions (Bernstein-Lange). Nonuniform branch distributions (e.g. Hamming-weight selection on Koblitz curves) need the general sum p_i^2 form: ECC2K-130 walk factor 1.069993 with 8 scalars.

cited_by.note: first-order walk model 1/sqrt(1 - sum p^2) (Teske; Brent-Pollard)

nodes.label: Bernstein-Lange: higher-degree local anti-collisions slow rho beyond Brent-Pollard
nodes.statement: Degree-k local anti-collisions add further nonrandomness: for p_i = 1/r the degree<=2 factor is 1/sqrt(1 - 1/r - 1/r^2 + 1/r^3); for r = 6 the factors rise from 1.095445 (degree 1) to a limit of 1.129162, and experiments on uniform random 6-step walks give 1.150103 (ell = 1009) falling to 1.129580 (ell = 10000000019) times sqrt(pi ell/2).
nodes.scope: Heuristic factors backed by about 230 experiments per ell; the authors do not know whether a quantitative analysis predicts the small-ell excess.

nodes.label: Teske: r-adding walks with r >= 20 behave like random walks
nodes.statement: Using Hildebrand's results, an r-adding walk should approximate the uniform distribution in fewer than sqrt r steps once r >= 6; Teske recommends r >= 20 and conjectures expected cycle length <= 1.3 sqrt r (against the random 1.2533 sqrt r). Sattler-Schnorr show, subject to a conjecture, that r >= 8 gives c sqrt(pi r/2) for an explicit c. Teske's experiments show the original three-branch walk is somewhat worse than random.
nodes.scope: Experimental and conjectural; the common practice r = 16 or 20 rests on it. BKL argue large r slows real implementations (cache), trading against nonrandomness and negation cycles.
nodes.formula: E[cycle length] <= 1.3 sqrt r for r >= 20 (conjectured)
source_locations: Bernstein-Lange 2013 Section 3.1 ('a common choice, recommended in [Teske], is |I| = 20')

nodes.label: Hildebrand: random r-step walks on Z/n mix in O(n^(2/(r-1)))
nodes.statement: Almost every r-adding walk on Z/ell (uniform step probabilities, random step set) reaches a nearly uniform distribution within O(ell^(2/(r-1))) steps, which is o(sqrt ell) for r >= 6.
nodes.scope: A mixing statement for random step sets; it does not by itself bound the collision time or its constant.

nodes.label: No rigorous sqrt bound for r-adding (doubling-free) rho walks
nodes.statement: The rigorous rho collision theorems (Miller-Venkatesan, KMT, KMPT) need the squaring/doubling branch; for the r-adding walks used in every large ECDLP computation there is no proof of an O(sqrt r) collision time, even in the random-partition model, only Hildebrand-type mixing and heuristics.
nodes.scope: Open in the cited literature as read; Miller-Venkatesan state that without squaring the mixing time of their graph would be exponential in log n.

nodes.label: Rigorous constant for implemented rho is open
nodes.statement: No proof gives the (sqrt(pi/2) + o(1)) sqrt r constant, or any constant within a small factor of it, for rho with an implementable (keyed-hash) partition; the best proved constant (KMPT, random oracle partition) is 52.5. Galbraith states a rigorous analysis of distributed rho is open.
nodes.scope: Every matched-rho reference therefore rests on HEUR-GG-DP-RHO and measurement, not on a theorem.
source_locations: Galbraith 2018 Section 14.2.5, p. 296 and Section 14.3.1, p. 298

nodes.label: Two grumpy giants and a baby beats rho on average (high memory)
nodes.statement: After (1.5 + o(1)) sqrt ell multiplications, BSGS succeeds with probability 0.5625 + o(1), a truly random walk with 0.6753... + o(1), and the two-grumpy-giants-and-a-baby method with 0.71875 + o(1). Experiments give average chain weights 1.23046 ell^1.5 (ell = 65537) and 1.20545 ell^1.5 (ell = 1000003), i.e. average cost below rho's sqrt(pi/2) = 1.2533 sqrt ell.
nodes.scope: Counts multiplications only; needs BSGS-like memory, no low-memory variant known; the average-case advantage is experimental. Shows rho is not an optimal generic algorithm even if perfectly random ('global anti-collisions').
nodes.formula: success after 1.5 sqrt(ell): 0.71875 (grumpy) vs 0.6753 (random walk) vs 0.5625 (BSGS)
non_implications: No low-memory version, so no improvement for large parallel ECDLP computations

nodes.label: Kangaroo heuristic (Galbraith Heur. 14.5.4)
nodes.statement: Walks reach distinguished points without cycles; kangaroo footprints are uniformly distributed with about one per interval of the mean step m; tame and wild walks are independent before colliding. Under it the DP kangaroo needs (2 + o(1)) sqrt w group operations on average (Theorem 14.5.5); parallel herds give (2 + o(1)) sqrt(w)/N_P per client (Heuristic 14.6.1, Theorem 14.6.2).
nodes.scope: Pollard showed the bound with o(1) replaced by some epsilon < 0.06; Montenegro-Tetali make it rigorous for power-of-2 jumps in the random-selection model.

nodes.label: Montenegro-Tetali: kangaroo takes (2 + o(1)) sqrt(b - a)
nodes.statement: If h = g^x with x uniform in [a, b], the distinguished-points kangaroo method uses (2 + o(1)) sqrt(b - a) expected group operations; the maximum, at x = a or b, is (3 + o(1)) sqrt(b - a). Lead constants are sharp (matching upper and lower bounds), and the result holds for step sizes powers of any fixed n (Pollard's conjecture).
nodes.scope: Random selection function and well-distributed distinguished points (Galbraith 14.5.6). Covers the two-kangaroo method, not the three-, four- or five-kangaroo variants.
nodes.formula: average (2 + o(1)) sqrt(b-a); worst (3 + o(1)) sqrt(b-a)

nodes.label: Galbraith-Pollard-Ruprai: 4-kangaroo 1.714 sqrt N, hybrid 1.66 sqrt N
nodes.statement: Interval DLP of width N: three kangaroos (1.818 + o(1)) sqrt N, four kangaroos with even jumps (1.714 + o(1)) sqrt N (ePrint abstract 1.715), and a four-kangaroo/Gaudry-Schost hybrid (1.661 + o(1)) sqrt N (Galbraith's book: 1.660), all heuristic average cases.
nodes.scope: Heuristic; Fowler records that the running-time calculation assumes the rear kangaroo always takes the expected number of steps, with no bound found on the resulting approximation error (GPR experiments agree with the predictions). No rigorous analysis analogous to Montenegro-Tetali.
assumptions: Expected-step substitution in the running-time calculation

nodes.label: Fowler: five kangaroos at 1.737 sqrt N (not below four)
nodes.statement: A five-kangaroo configuration achieves an estimated (1.737 + o(1)) sqrt N average, beating the three-kangaroo 1.818 but not the four-kangaroo 1.714; Theorem 3.2 lower-bounds the expected time until the closest useful pair collides for any 5-kangaroo split into tame/wild1/wild2.
nodes.scope: Same heuristic substitution as GPR, error unbounded; whether more than four kangaroos can beat 1.714 remains open in the thesis.

nodes.label: Rho on equivalence classes: sqrt(pi r/(2 N_C)) (C1 + C2)
nodes.statement: If each class of generic size N_C has a computable unique representative and induced (a, b), rho on classes needs (sqrt(pi/(2 N_C)) + o(1)) sqrt r (C1 + C2) bit operations (C1 group operation, C2 canonicalization), ignoring useless cycles; with n_S = log r the cycle-handling overhead is o(sqrt r) and storage O(log r).
nodes.scope: Conditional on a class analogue of Heuristic 14.2.15 and on ignoring fruitless cycles; the gain needs C2 < C1, since naive canonicalization costs O~(N_C).
assumptions: Class version of the DP rho heuristic
Useless cycles ignored or handled at negligible cost

nodes.label: Fruitless-cycle rates: 2-cycles Theta(1/r), 2c-cycles Theta(1/r^c)
nodes.statement: For a negating additive walk with r branches, a fruitless 2-cycle starts with probability about 1/(2r) per step (generally 1/(N_C n_S) for classes of size N_C), 4-cycles with probability Theta(1/r^2), and length-2c cycles with probability roughly proportional to 1/r^c (Duursma-Gaudry-Morain Appendix A).
nodes.scope: Heuristic, assuming a perfectly random selection function and representative; with r = 2048 a walk without 4-cycle handling expects a cycle within millions of steps.

cited_by.note: 2-cycle rates per 10^6 steps for +-R arms at r = 1024

nodes.label: Certicom 1998: normalizing distinguished points alone gives sqrt 2 / sqrt(2d)
nodes.statement: A Certicom web page of 23 March 1998 claimed a sqrt(2d) speedup for Koblitz curves over F_2^d from normalizing x-coordinates of distinguished points modulo powers of the Frobenius sigma, and a sqrt 2 speedup for general curves from normalizing modulo negation.
nodes.scope: Refuted two weeks later by Wiener-Zuccherato: normalizing only the stored distinguished points gives no speedup unless the walk itself is well-defined on the classes.
source_locations: Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe 2011 Appendix A ('Multiplicative walks' and following)

nodes.label: Quotient speedup requires a walk well-defined on classes
nodes.statement: A collision search gains the factor sqrt(N_C) only if the iteration is a function of the equivalence class (it maps the class representative, so all members of a class follow the same path); canonicalizing only the stored distinguished points leaves the number of distinct states and hence the collision time unchanged.
nodes.scope: Elementary counting; stated by Wiener-Zuccherato (as reported) and built into Galbraith's class walk (14.6).

nodes.label: Wiener-Zuccherato negating additive walk with 2-cycle look-back
nodes.statement: An additive walk on {P, -P} classes that detects 2-cycles by comparing h(W_{i+1}) with h(W_i) and retroactively incrementing the hash, claimed to give a sqrt 2 speedup for any curve and sqrt(2d) on Koblitz curves over F_2^d.
nodes.scope: 4-cycles (and longer) are neither detected nor escaped, so a walk cycles within Theta(r^2) steps; the method only works with distinguished-point frequency well above 1/r^2, which for large ell causes communication and storage blow-up (BLS).
source_locations: Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe 2011 Appendix A ('Additive walks with 2-cycle detection and hash modification')

nodes.label: BKL 2010: negation gives little or no speedup on SIMD
nodes.statement: Bos-Kleinjung-Lenstra found that most negating rho algorithms in the literature were non-functional, that across 126 combinations of cycle-handling options the best non-SIMD speedup was far below sqrt 2, and that on SIMD-parallel walks it is 'a challenge to achieve any speedup at all' because cycle handling needs branching.
nodes.scope: The non-functionality finding stands for the methods they tested; the SIMD impossibility claim was refuted by the branchless method of Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe, which measured close to sqrt 2 on the PS3. BLS also dispute BKL's reading of Gallant-Lambert-Vanstone (GLV did not specify the escape iteration BKL attribute to them).
source_locations: Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe 2011 Section 1 (quoting [6]) and Appendix A ('More possibilities')

nodes.label: BLS branchless negating rho: (1+o(1)) sqrt(pi ell/4)
nodes.statement: Walk W_{i+1} = |W_i + R_h(W_i)| with sparse periodic checks for 2-cycles (every about 2 sqrt r steps), 4-, 6-, ... cycles up to length about log(ell)/log(r), escaping by doubling the lexicographic minimum, all done branch-free; it uses (1+o(1)) sqrt(pi ell/4) iterations of one EC addition each under standard heuristics. Fruitless cycles cost a factor 1 + Theta(1/sqrt r), larger than the Theta(1/r) r-adding nonrandomness, both vanishing as r -> infinity. Measured on secp112r1-shaped curves: 33791 runs on a 60-bit group gave 0.9996 of the predicted distinguished-point count; about twice the speed of the earlier PS3 record.
nodes.scope: Heuristic iteration count confirmed experimentally at 2^60 scale; r = 2048, 2-cycle check every 48 steps, 12-cycle check every 49152 steps in their software.
assumptions: Random-walk heuristic for the negating additive walk
nodes.formula: E[iterations] = (1+o(1)) sqrt(pi ell/4); overhead 1 + Theta(1/sqrt r)

cited_by.note: negation map: fruitless-cycle detection and escape are not priced

nodes.label: Gallant-Lambert-Vanstone multiplicative walk on Frobenius-negation orbits
nodes.statement: On a group with efficient endomorphism psi of order m acting as x -> x^lambda, step x_{i+1} = (1 + psi^j) x_i with j chosen from the class representative; the map is well-defined on classes {psi^j(x)}, generally avoids short fruitless cycles, and on Koblitz curves over F_2^m with classes {+-pi^i(P)} gives about sqrt(pi 2^m/(4m)) group operations (a sqrt(2m) speedup).
nodes.scope: Heuristic random-walk analysis; less flexibility in walk design; selection via Hamming weight of the normal-basis x-coordinate is nonuniform and costs a Brent-Pollard factor (1.069993 for the ECC2K-130 walk).
assumptions: No short multiplicative relations among the scalars 1 + lambda^j
nodes.formula: ~ sqrt(pi 2^m / (4m)) group operations on Koblitz curves

edges.statement: Nechaev's bound is for deterministic algorithms, so it says nothing about randomized rho; Shoup's randomized-encoding model is needed.
Shoup extends the Omega(sqrt r) bound from deterministic to probabilistic generic algorithms with random encodings.
In Maurer's label-free model the birthday bound holds only if equality queries are free or a total-order oracle is added; rho itself needs the ordering oracle.
Shoup and Maurer models agree on single-stage games but separate on some multi-stage games, so generic bounds must name their model.
Schnorr-family proofs in the joint generic+random-oracle model avoid forking reductions but inherit both idealizations.
The equivalences are statements about algebraic adversaries.
In the AGM the generic CDH-to-DL reduction becomes an equivalence (DL also reduces to CDH for algebraic adversaries).
The transfer combines these AGM reductions with the generic DL bound.
The GGM DL lower bound is the other ingredient of the transfer.
KZZ exhibit cases where AGM hardness does not imply GGM hardness under current formalizations: published disagreement with FKL.
The transfer holds under the Jaeger-Mohan interpretation; it rests on that framework (published reply to KZZ).
Jaeger-Mohan argue KZZ adopted an interpretation under which the FKL claim fails, and give one under which it holds.
An AGM security proof does not guarantee that any concrete group instantiates the scheme securely.
The AGM forces algebraic outputs; an ECDLP algorithm using coordinate algebra (summation polynomials, descent) need not be algebraic in this sense, so AGM statements do not exclude it.
Yun's Omega(sqrt(n p)) generic bound shows the Kuhn-Struik shared-table rho is asymptotically optimal for n targets (within Yun's parameter range).
Closes the uniform generic part of the multi-target question: sqrt(n p) total, sqrt(p/n) per target, nothing better generically without preprocessing.
Concrete amortization: per-target cost falls like 1/sqrt(L) when the DP table is kept, so single-target sqrt(r) does not price many-key adversaries.
The sqrt(2 r L) estimate is a random-mapping birthday computation.
With free precomputation of ~ell^(2/3) the online cost is ~ell^(1/3) in the RAM metric (P-256: ~2^86), which is the non-uniform crack in standard concrete-security definitions.
S T^2 = Omega~(eps N): with S ~ ell^(1/3) stored points the online time cannot go below ~ell^(1/3), so the Bernstein-Lange attack is optimal in the generic preprocessing model.
P T + T^2 = Omega(eps N) forces precomputation P ~ ell^(2/3) for T ~ ell^(1/3), matching the 2^170 P-256 table cost.
Success probability ~0.23 per online walk is computed assuming random-walk coverage of the precomputed points.
Time-only security definitions admit the non-uniform ell^(1/3) algorithm; Bernstein-Lange show AT cost restores ~sqrt(ell).
Re-derives the CGK auxiliary-input DL/DH bounds with presampling (bit-fixing) proofs and extends them to further assumptions.
Alternative reduction-based proofs of preprocessing GGM bounds in the bit-fixing model.
AHP give direct GGM proofs for several results previously obtained through the AGM, sidestepping the disputed transfer for those results.
The small-DL paper is the measured, tuned instance of the precomputed-distinguished-point method (table ell^(1/3), online ~1.77 ell^(1/3)).
With precomputation the interval DLP drops from ~sqrt(w) to 1.93 w^(1/3) per instance.
Theorem 14.2.23 (Miller-Venkatesan Thm 1.1) is a probability over uniformly random partitions; it does not apply to a keyed-hash partition.
The O(log^3 n) mixing time of the rho graph is the key input to the O(sqrt n log^3 n) collision bound.
Mixing is for the Markov chain induced by a random partition.
KMT analyse the idealization in which each element is assigned independently and uniformly to a branch.
KMPT Theorem 4.2 assumes the partition is given by a random oracle (Remark 2.1).
Nondegeneracy is proved for random partitions and a random start.
Improves log^3 to log * loglog in the collision bound.
The Markov-chain birthday paradox gives an additive (not multiplicative) mixing term, which yields Theta(sqrt|G|).
Removes the log factor: Theta(sqrt|G|) with explicit constant 52.5.
Rigorous O(sqrt|G|) expected collision time for the three-branch walk in the random-oracle-partition model.
Turns a collision into a solved DLP with probability 1 - o(1) for almost every prime order, completing the runtime proof.
KMPT Section 5 proves Theta(sqrt(|G|)/J) per processor for distinguished points (random partition), an issue Galbraith 14.3.1 lists as open for the implemented method.
Heuristic constant sqrt(pi/2) = 1.2533 vs proved 52.5: the rigorous result confirms the order but leaves a ~42x gap in the constant.
The (1.253 + o(1)) sqrt r cost used for implemented DP rho is Theorem 14.2.16 under Heuristic 14.2.15.
Part 2 of Heuristic 14.2.15 is the random-mapping birthday count.
Injective-per-branch walks are less random than a random mapping: multiply the birthday constant by 1/sqrt(1 - sum p_i^2).
Brent-Pollard captures only degree-1 anti-collisions; for r = 6 the predicted factor is 1.129 not 1.095, and experiments agree with the larger value. Published correction of the standard heuristic.
Teske's r >= 6 near-uniformity argument uses Hildebrand's mixing result.
Even for r = 20 the Brent-Pollard factor 1/sqrt(1 - 1/20) = 1.026 remains; BLS note that the PS3 record's r = 16 walk made its sqrt(pi q/2) iteration estimate slightly too optimistic.
Implemented EC rho uses r-adding walks; its sqrt(pi r/2) cost is the random-walk constant times the Teske/Brent-Pollard factor, both heuristic.
No theorem bounds the collision time of doubling-free r-adding walks.
The spectral argument relies on the squaring branch; Miller-Venkatesan note mixing would be exponential in log n without it.
The heuristic constant 1.253 for implemented DP rho has no proof; rigorous constants are ~42x larger and only for random partitions.
Distributed rho has no rigorous analysis for implementable walks (Galbraith 14.3.1).

Rho is not an optimal generic method even if perfectly random: global anti-collisions leave a gap that a high-memory method closes (0.71875 vs 0.6753 success at 1.5 sqrt ell; experimental average ~1.205 sqrt ell).
Same memory class as BSGS, with strictly more distinct slopes per multiplication.
Any generic method stays Omega(sqrt ell); Bernstein-Lange note BSGS and rho are within a factor 2 + o(1) of the constant-level generic bound.
The O(sqrt W) kangaroo cost in the corpus is Galbraith Theorem 14.5.5 under Heuristic 14.5.4.
Rigorous (2 + o(1)) sqrt(b-a) average and (3 + o(1)) worst case for the DP kangaroo with power-of-n jumps (random selection).
Makes the footprint heuristic's conclusion rigorous with sharp lead constants, in the random-selection model.
Three/four-kangaroo constants are computed from the footprint heuristic.
Lower heuristic constants 1.818 / 1.714 / 1.661 against 2 for the classical kangaroo.
The 1.661 hybrid combines Gaudry-Schost tame/wild regions with the four-kangaroo even-jump trick.
Same heuristic substitution as the GPR analysis.
Five kangaroos (1.737) beat three (1.818) but not four (1.714); Fowler notes the GPR running-time computation has an unbounded approximation error.
Galbraith Theorem 14.4.3 is the precise conditional form of the sqrt(N_C) heuristic, with canonicalization cost C2 made explicit.
The theorem's walk (14.6) is defined on class representatives; without that no speedup occurs.
Normalizing only distinguished points leaves the walk and its collision time unchanged (Wiener-Zuccherato, as reported by BLS).
With classes the 2-cycle rate is 1/(N_C n_S) per step, so fruitless cycles appear regularly unless handled; the theorem ignores them.
Quantifies the obstruction: 2-cycles Theta(1/r), 2c-cycles Theta(1/r^c).
4-cycles at Theta(1/r^2) are not handled by the Wiener-Zuccherato rule, so walks cycle within Theta(r^2) steps.
A branch-free negating walk with periodic cycle checks and doubling escapes measured close to sqrt 2 on the SIMD Cell processor, contradicting BKL's SIMD claim.
Shows the fruitless-cycle obstruction costs only 1 + Theta(1/sqrt r), negligible as r grows, when cycles are checked on a sparse schedule.
The negation map (N_C = 2) case of automorphism-folded rho, with a costed cycle-handling rule.
The check schedule (2-cycles every ~2 sqrt r steps) and the 1 + Theta(1/sqrt r) overhead are derived from the cycle-rate heuristic.
The (1+o(1)) sqrt(pi ell/4) count assumes the quotient walk behaves randomly.
Frobenius-and-negation orbits of size 2m on Koblitz curves.
A multiplicative walk well-defined on classes avoids short fruitless cycles when the scalars 1 + lambda^j have no short relations, at the cost of walk flexibility.
Hamming-weight branch selection is nonuniform: the ECC2K-130 walk pays 1.069993 (degree 1) and about 1.0786 (degree <= 2).
The first published sqrt 2 claim for general curves, which needs high distinguished-point frequency and does not scale to large ell.
BKL found most published negating algorithms (WZ-style and others) non-functional in the claimed time; that finding is not refuted by BLS.

research_targets.label: Measure rho walk nonrandomness against Brent-Pollard and BL higher-degree predictions
research_targets.objective: For the repository's actual rho walks (r-adding with r = 16, 20, 1024, 2048; negating; the ECC2K-130 Frobenius walk) measure steps to first useful collision divided by sqrt(pi N/2) and compare with 1/sqrt(1 - sum p^2) and the Bernstein-Lange all-degree factor (r = 6: 1.129162).
research_targets.acceptance: An ecbench session with interleaved arms per walk at three or more group sizes, paired bootstrap intervals on the factor, and a statement of which prediction each interval contains.
research_targets.next_step: Freeze a spec with the walk list above at N ~ 2^32-2^40 and run it through the standard ecbench measurement route.
research_targets.notes: Matched-rho references in the leaderboard use the idealized constant; the walk factor shifts every gap by a few percent.

research_targets.label: Price fruitless-cycle handling in the negation-map rho
research_targets.objective: Measure the per-step overhead of 2-, 4- and longer-cycle checks and escapes as a function of r and check it against the BLS 1 + Theta(1/sqrt r) prediction and the DGM rates; then price it in hwcost/rho.rs, where it is currently unpriced.
research_targets.acceptance: Measured cycle-entry rates per 10^6 steps for each cycle length and r, the fitted overhead coefficient, and a priced negation arm whose speedup over the plain walk has an interval.
research_targets.next_step: Reuse the rho_walk_leads_20261014 counters (cycles_length_2/4) at r = 256, 1024, 2048, 4096.

research_targets.label: Prove (or bound) collision time of doubling-free r-adding walks
research_targets.objective: In the random-partition model, prove an O(sqrt N) (ideally explicit-constant) collision bound for r-adding walks on Z/N with r fixed, combining Hildebrand mixing with the KMPT Markov-chain birthday theorem, or show where the argument breaks.
research_targets.acceptance: A written proof checked by a second reader, or an explicit obstruction (e.g. a family of step sets where the L-infinity decay condition of KMPT Theorem 3.2 fails).
research_targets.next_step: Check whether Hildebrand's 'almost every step set' statement gives the pointwise decay KMPT Theorem 3.2 needs for r >= 6.

research_targets.label: Close the 52.5 vs 1.2533 rho constant gap
research_targets.objective: Tighten the KMPT explicit constant for the three-branch walk (or a variant with x -> x^l steps) toward sqrt(pi/2), so that matched-rho references rest on a theorem in the random-oracle-partition model.
research_targets.acceptance: A proved expected-collision constant below 52.5 with its hypotheses, or a lower bound showing the three-branch walk's constant exceeds sqrt(pi/2).
research_targets.next_step: Measure the three-branch walk's actual constant numerically (exact Markov chain on small prime N) to see how far it is from both.
